title: Module 14 Challenge: Predict and Explain
scenario: An advisor predicts first-year GPA from two variables for 40 students: weekly study hours and high school GPA. Together the predictors give R squared = .30, F(2, 37) = 7.93, p = .001. The advisor tells a student, "You need about five more hours of studying a week to raise your GPA by half a point, because the model proves that studying causes higher grades."

parts.q: What does R squared = .30 mean here?
o: The two predictors together account for 30 percent of the variability in GPA
The model predicts 30 percent of students correctly
parts.why: Seventy percent of the variability is left unexplained.

parts.q: Which statement about the omnibus F is correct?
o: It shows the predictors together explain more than zero variability
It shows each predictor is significant
It shows that studying causes higher grades
It shows the model is perfect

parts.q: Evaluate the advisor's statement. Address causation, the limit of prediction for one student, and the risk of extrapolating, and offer a better wording.
parts.model: The advisor treats a prediction model as a causal one. The data are observational, so students who study more might also be more motivated or better prepared, and high school GPA is already in the model for a reason. R squared of .30 means 70 percent of the variability in GPA is unexplained, so predictions for any one student carry a lot of error and the standard error of estimate should be reported. Promising a half-point gain also assumes a straight line continues beyond the range of the data, which is extrapolation. A better statement is "Among students like those we studied, those who study more tend to have higher GPAs after accounting for high school GPA, but individual results vary widely."
check: I said the model does not show causation
I noted the large unexplained variability for an individual
I mentioned extrapolation or the linearity assumption
My rewrite described tendencies and variation
